newsitem.title: UK: Women need not die giving birth - pressure group.
newsitem.headline: Women need not die giving birth - pressure group.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of women around the world die each year from mostly preventable causes relating to pregnancy and childbirth, the International Planned Parenthood Federation said on Thursday (IPPF).

"Every year 650,000 women die from pregnancy related causes - deaths that could be prevented," IPPF Secretary General Ingar Brueggemann said a news conference. "A woman has a right to survive if she gets pregnant."

Brueggeman was speaking at the launch of the London based pressure group's "Charter on Sexual and Reproductive Rights" initiative which aims to raise global awareness of the plight of women who the IPPF says are being denied basic human rights.
The charter identifies "reproductive rights" which the group, which represents family planning organisations in 140 countries, says are either not wholly recognised or enforced.
These rights include access to affordable healthcare and information on contraception.

"These rights have already been adopted by at least 100 countries but in many cases the commitment is not being enforced," Brueggeman said, adding that in some African nations people can be imprisoned for trying to set up such an organisation.
"There is just no excuse for this behaviour," she said.
She said in some Asian and African countries girls as young as 12 were being "forced" into marriage and having children.
The IPPF charter is not just applicable to Third World nations Brueggeman said. "Some states in the U.S. are engaged in trying to overturn U.S. law governing access to abortions."
Bruggeman said the IPPF did not advocate abortion as a means of planned parenthood. "But what we do say is as a last resort, women should have access to a safe abortion," she said.
A leading British anti-abortion group dismissed the IPPF's initiative as a "charter for more abortions."
"The fact is that the majority of abortions are done for social rather than medical reasons," said Brendan Gerrard, spokesman for the Society for the Protection of Unborn Children.
